title: Plan seasonal PR around an audience need, not just a calendar date
shortdescription: Build a seasonal pitch around a useful answer, credible evidence and a clear deadline. A worked example shows how to turn that brief into a campaign.
description:
PRSA’s measurement guidance puts audience research before campaign planning and asks communicators to define success before selecting messages and channels. Applied to seasonal PR, this means identifying a real decision your audience faces.

For example, a back-to-school campaign could answer how families compare recurring costs, rather than merely announcing a seasonal discount. The supporting material might include an itemized example, a clearly described survey or a specialist available to explain the tradeoffs. Do not manufacture a trend to justify the pitch.

Write down the audience, the question, the evidence, the spokesperson and the date the information stops being useful. Work backward from journalists’ actual deadlines; there is no universal lead time for every publication. Confirm that quoted prices, stock and service capacity can support the campaign.

Choose a result you can evaluate, such as qualified enquiries or use of a resource. Track coverage separately from that result, and compare performance with the objective agreed at the start. A seasonal hook earns attention only when the underlying information deserves it.

Consider a fictional retailer preparing for back-to-school shopping. “Our sale starts Monday” gives a journalist little to work with. A more useful brief would compare the total cost of a defined school-supply basket, state which items are included, explain the comparison date and make a buyer available to discuss the tradeoffs.

The pitch can then lead with the audience’s decision: what must be bought now, what can be reused and where a cheaper item may create a later replacement cost. If the retailer cannot substantiate a comparison, narrow the claim to its own documented prices. Describe the commercial interest openly and provide the underlying calculation.

Before sending the pitch, name the person who will answer follow-up questions and confirm when the prices expire. After publication, track use of the comparison resource and relevant enquiries alongside coverage. If the campaign generated attention but readers could not find the promised information, improve that resource before repeating the promotion.
takeaways: Start with a decision the audience needs to make.
Supply evidence a reader or journalist can inspect.
Measure use of the information alongside the coverage it receives.

title: Freedom 250 performer withdrawals show why event positioning must be explicit
shortdescription: Freedom 250’s performer withdrawals offer a lesson for event organizers: agree on political positioning, promotion and participant approval before announcing a lineup.
description:
PolitiFact’s June 1 account described a May 27 announcement of nine musical acts for Freedom 250 events scheduled from June 25 to July 3. It reported that most subsequently withdrew, with several expressing concern about politicization. The account also documented Donald Trump’s suggestion that a rally replace musical performances.

That record supports a story about announced plans and withdrawals. It does not justify treating every proposed replacement or later event detail as settled.

An event brief should make the organizer, funding, political involvement and intended use of a performer’s name clear before promotion begins. Written agreement on those points reduces the chance that participants learn about material positioning through publicity.

When a lineup changes, publish a dated correction in the places where the original appeared and distinguish confirmed performers from invitations. For audiences, an archived announcement is not a reliable guide to a final schedule. This analysis concerns the communications process, not a judgment about an artist’s political views.
